# Commute ping: how we chose the trigger and ceiling (1.25x / 1.25x)

Status: decision record. Written after the choice was made, to document every setting we compared, the data behind each, and why 1.25x / 1.25x was picked. Applies to PRD section 8 (Push Surface).

**Important caveat up front.** Every percentage below comes from the project's *synthetic* fare history (generated by `eval/generate_data.py`, hand-built rush-hour curve). They describe how the *rule behaves on the simulation*, not how often real riders would be pinged. See "What this does and does not prove" at the end.

---

> **Update (2026-11-19):** Sections 4-10 were computed on the earlier dataset, where each ride type was a scaled copy of one route forecast. The fare history now has real per-ride-type rows. Cab (Standard) behaves essentially as before; auto changed little; the two-wheeler changed a lot. Section 13 and 14 re-run the rain/event cases and the rule comparison on the new data, and the conclusion (1.25x / 1.25x) holds.

## 1. The feature being tuned

A rider sets a usual commute time per direction (to work, and back). **One ping per direction per day is sent 45 minutes before the usual time**, only if the surge forecast says it will help:

- **Trigger (a):** the forecast multiplier for the rider's usual ride type at the usual time is at least `T`.
- **Ceiling (b):** the forecast multiplier 30 minutes before the usual time (the time the ping tells the rider to start by) is at most `C`.
- The ping text carries no multiplier: "<Ride type> fares to <destination> are likely to be high around <usual time>. Start by <usual time minus 30 min> to avoid the surge."
- The ping must land at least 15 minutes before the advised start; nothing is sent before 6:00am.

The decision was the pair `(T, C)`. Final choice: **T = 1.25x, C = 1.25x**.

## 2. How the design got here (decisions in order)

1. Original idea: pings 90 and 30 minutes before, reporting surge or "no surge as of now". Review found problems:
   - "Book now" cannot work for a ride at 9:00 (Uber's price is set when you request).
   - A surge reading now says little about surge at departure; the ping should be about the forecast at departure.
   - "No surge" messages are noise and train riders to mute the app.
   - A single fixed time is fragile (work-from-home days, holidays), so setup asks for days of the week and offers a pause.
   - Each direction needs its own pickup, drop, time.
2. Product-owner decisions: no "no surge" ping; permission asked at the end of setup; max one ping per direction per day; **one ping, 45 minutes before**; advice is simply "start 30 minutes earlier", with no multiplier in the text.
3. Open question: what trigger and ceiling make "start 30 minutes earlier" both *true* and *not noisy*?

## 3. Method

- **Data:** 5 routes, simulated weekday history (about 137,000 rows). The forecast is the production engine: median of comparable trips within +/-45 minutes (widening if thin), clipped 0.5x to 2.0x, anything under 1.05x shown as 1.0x (normal pricing).
- **Ride types:** the multiplier is per ride type. Autos feel about 55% of the route surge, cabs (standard, sedan, six-seater) 100%, two-wheelers 25%.
- **Grid:** every usual time in 15-minute steps, 6:00-11:00 and 16:00-21:00, for each route, dry and rain.
- **Metric used throughout:** "share of commute times that would get a ping" = pings fired / usual times checked. A rider's usual time is fixed, so in practice this is "what share of riders (by commute time) ever get pinged on a typical day", not a random chance per day.
- Later checks used a Python port of the engine (parity-checked against the app) to regenerate the data at different seeds, sizes and ramp shapes.

## 4. Round 1: trigger alone, and trigger plus "cheaper by 0.1x"

Share of peak commute times where the forecast at the usual time is at least T (cabs, all routes, weekday):

| Trigger T | Morning | Evening |
|---|---|---|
| 1.05x | 95% | 98% |
| 1.10x | 92% | 97% |
| 1.25x | 81% | 91% |

Finding: a trigger alone fires on almost every peak commute (noise). Adding "starting 30 minutes earlier is cheaper by at least 0.1x" cut it to about 37% (T = 1.1x) and 33-34% (T = 1.25x). Conclusion: a second condition on the earlier time is needed.

## 5. Round 2: absolute ceiling on the earlier time (T = 1.25x, cabs, 30-minute shift)

Share of commute times that get a ping, by ceiling `C`:

| Ceiling C | Morning dry | Evening dry | Morning rain | Evening rain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.10x | 2% | 2% | 1% | 0% |
| 1.15x | 4% | 3% | 1% | 1% |
| 1.20x | 7% | 7% | 4% | 2% |
| 1.25x | 8% | 10% | 7% | 4% |

Of the times when surge at the usual time is already 1.25x or more, the share that get a ping:

| Ceiling C | Morning dry | Evening dry | Morning rain | Evening rain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.10x | 5% | 3% | 1% | 0% |
| 1.15x | 10% | 5% | 1% | 1% |
| 1.20x | 17% | 11% | 4% | 2% |
| 1.25x | 19% | 16% | 7% | 4% |

Per route (dry, both peaks): at 1.10x, two routes get pings some of the time and three get none (5%, 0%, 0%, 5%, 0%). At 1.25x four routes get about 10% and the fifth about 5%.

Per ride type, dry, both peaks: at 1.25x ceiling: two-wheeler 0%, three-wheeler (auto) 7%, standard / sedan / six-seater 9%. At 1.10x: 0%, 0%, 2%, 2%, 2%.

Finding: a 1.1x ceiling makes the feature almost silent; a 1.25x ceiling gives roughly one working day in ten for a rider on the rising edge of a peak.

## 6. Round 3: could a longer "start earlier" window help? (T = 1.25x, cabs)

Share of commute times that get a ping if the rider were asked to start 30, 45 or 60 minutes earlier:

| Start earlier by | Ceiling | Morning dry | Evening dry | Morning rain | Evening rain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 min | 1.10x | 2% | 2% | 1% | 0% |
| 30 min | 1.20x | 7% | 7% | 4% | 2% |
| 30 min | 1.25x | 8% | 10% | 7% | 4% |
| 45 min | 1.10x | 5% | 6% | 2% | 0% |
| 45 min | 1.20x | 10% | 11% | 6% | 3% |
| 45 min | 1.25x | 11% | 14% | 10% | 6% |
| 60 min | 1.10x | 8% | 10% | 6% | 0% |
| 60 min | 1.20x | 14% | 16% | 10% | 4% |
| 60 min | 1.25x | 15% | 19% | 15% | 8% |

Finding: a longer window raises the share, but the ping is sent 45 minutes before the usual time and must land at least 15 minutes before the advised start, so a 45- or 60-minute "start earlier" is not possible. The window stays 30 minutes.

## 7. Round 4: the product owner's trial of 1.4x

Two settings were tried: T = 1.4x with C = 1.25x, then T = 1.4x with C = 1.4x.

**T = 1.4x, C = 1.25x** (share of commute times that get a ping):

| Vehicle | Morning dry | Evening dry | Morning rain | Evening rain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auto | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| Cab | 2% | 3% | 0% | 0% |
| Two-wheeler | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |

How often the usual-time condition alone is met (forecast of 1.4x or more): auto 5% / 11% / 30% / 44% and cab 26% / 43% / 70% / 81% (morning dry / evening dry / morning rain / evening rain). The highest an auto ever reaches in the simulation is 1.55x.

Of the times a cab is at 1.4x or more at the usual time, the forecast 30 minutes earlier is *also* 1.4x or more in 78-91% of cases (so no ping), between 1.25x and 1.4x in 9-15%, and at or below 1.25x only in 0-7%. For autos: also 1.4x or more in 60-83%, between 1.25x and 1.4x in 17-40%, at or below 1.25x never.

**T = 1.4x, C = 1.4x:**

| Vehicle | Morning dry | Evening dry | Morning rain | Evening rain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auto | 2% | 4% | 8% | 8% |
| Cab | 6% | 9% | 8% | 8% |

Finding: with C = 1.4x the advice becomes weak. When a ping fires, the earlier start is cheaper by a median of only 0.17x for cabs and 0.10x for autos, and sometimes by as little as 0.04x, so "start earlier to avoid the surge" can be untrue (the earlier time can itself be 1.38x). A high trigger also leaves auto riders almost never pinged.

## 8. Round 5: is it just a sample-size problem?

We regenerated the data with 5 random seeds at 28,000 rows per route (current, 137k in total), 84,000 (3x) and 280,000 (10x, about 1.37M rows), on a finer 5-minute grid. Mean share of commute times pinged (dry, weekday):

| Rule | Time | 137k rows | 410k rows | 1.37M rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cab 1.25 / 1.10 | Morning | 1.8% | 2.4% | 2.2% |
| Cab 1.25 / 1.10 | Evening | 2.4% | 2.2% | 2.4% |
| Cab 1.25 / 1.25 | Morning | 8.1% | 8.5% | 8.3% |
| Cab 1.25 / 1.25 | Evening | 10.4% | 10.5% | 10.4% |
| Cab 1.40 / 1.25 | Morning | 2.4% | 2.2% | 2.2% |
| Cab 1.40 / 1.25 | Evening | 2.6% | 2.4% | 2.2% |
| Cab 1.40 / 1.40 | Morning | 7.5% | 6.8% | 6.9% |
| Cab 1.40 / 1.40 | Evening | 8.3% | 8.1% | 8.1% |
| Auto 1.25 / 1.25 | Morning | 5.9% | 5.9% | 5.9% |
| Auto 1.25 / 1.25 | Evening | 7.9% | 7.9% | 7.9% |
| Auto 1.40 / 1.40 | Morning | 2.0% | 2.0% | 2.0% |
| Auto 1.40 / 1.40 | Evening | 3.9% | 3.9% | 3.9% |

Seed-to-seed spread was about 1-3 percentage points. Finding: more synthetic rows do not change the picture. The forecast already uses 100+ comparable trips per cell, and the shape of the data comes from the hand-built curve, so more rows only reduce noise that was already small.

## 9. Round 6: does the shape of the rush-hour ramp matter?

We rebuilt the data with narrower and wider peaks (0.5x, 0.7x, 1.5x, 2x of the current width, same peak height) and with a smooth ramp that rises from 1.0x with no step at the start of the peak (our current data has a jump to 1.15x). Mean of morning and evening, 3 seeds, dry:

| Ramp | Cab 1.25/1.1 | Cab 1.25/1.25 | Cab 1.4/1.25 | Cab 1.4/1.4 | Auto 1.25/1.25 | Auto 1.4/1.4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Much steeper | 3.2% | 9.2% | 3.8% | 6.7% | 4.9% | 1.0% |
| Steeper | 3.0% | 9.2% | 3.4% | 7.3% | 6.8% | 1.0% |
| **Current** | 2.0% | 9.2% | 2.4% | 7.8% | 6.9% | 3.0% |
| Flatter | 1.6% | 10.6% | 1.6% | 8.6% | 6.9% | 3.0% |
| Much flatter | 0.9% | 7.6% | 0.4% | 7.5% | 6.9% | 3.9% |
| Smooth, steeper | 2.6% | 9.1% | 3.6% | 7.4% | 4.9% | 1.0% |
| Smooth, current width | 1.5% | 9.1% | 2.5% | 7.3% | 6.9% | 2.1% |
| Smooth, flatter | 0.7% | 11.0% | 1.0% | 8.7% | 6.9% | 3.0% |

Findings:
- Equal trigger and ceiling is robust: cab 1.25/1.25 stays between 7.6% and 11.0%, cab 1.4/1.4 between 6.7% and 8.7%.
- The strict ceilings are fragile: cab 1.25/1.1 ranges 0.7% to 3.2%, cab 1.4/1.25 ranges 0.4% to 3.8%.
- Auto 1.25/1.25 holds at about 5-7%; auto 1.4/1.4 swings from 1% to 3.9%.
- The ramp matters less than expected because the engine takes a median over a +/-45 minute window, which smooths any ramp.

## 10. Why 1.25x / 1.25x

1. **It is the only option that fires often enough to be demonstrable and useful for both cabs and autos** (about 7-11% of cab commute times, 5-7% for autos), while still being rare enough to avoid noise (roughly one working day in ten for a rider on the rising edge of a peak).
2. **It is robust.** The share barely moves across 5 seeds, 10x more rows, and 8 ramp shapes (cab 7.6-11.0%). The settings with a lower ceiling or a 1.4x trigger are the fragile ones.
3. **It reads simply:** ping when surge at the usual time is at least 1.25x and 30 minutes earlier is below 1.25x. Same number as the PRD's medium-risk line.
4. **The advice is mostly true.** In the 59 cases where it fires (cab and auto, dry and rain), the earlier start is cheaper by a median of 0.16x for cabs and 0.09x for autos.
5. **It covers rain.** With a 1.1x ceiling rain mornings got almost no pings (1%); at 1.25x they get about 7%.

### Known weakness of the chosen rule

Because the ceiling equals the trigger, the gap between the two times can be tiny. In the simulation, for cabs the earlier start was cheaper by 0.02x at the minimum (3 of 29 firing cases under 0.05x, 5 under 0.10x); for autos 0.04x at the minimum, and 22 of 30 cases under 0.10x (median 0.094x). So for autos the saving is often small. Options if this matters (not implemented): require a minimum gap of about 0.05-0.10x between the two times, or soften the wording to "fares may be lower if you start by <time>".

## 11. What this does and does not prove

- **Proves:** the rule is stable on the simulation, and the stricter rules we considered would almost never fire.
- **Does not prove:** how often real riders would be pinged. The rush-hour curve is hand-built, so the exact percentages describe our assumptions. If real ramps are steeper or flatter, the share changes (Section 9 suggests the equal-threshold rule moves only modestly).
- **Not tested:** weekends; event days; rain on top of peaks beyond the dry/rain split above; ping share by individual rider rather than by commute time; whether riders act on the advice; whether many riders reacting at once shifts the surge (the PRD already notes the feedback risk).
- **The result is also limited by the engine.** The forecast smooths over a 90-minute window, so it cannot see a sharp ramp inside a 30-minute step.
- For a resume or interview, quote this as "about 7-11% of commute times in simulation, robust to ramp shape", not as a measured real-world rate.

## 12. Reproducing

- Defaults live in `app/app-uber-ui.html` (`DEFAULT_RULES.pingThr`, `DEFAULT_RULES.earlierMax`) and the controls are in the Push alerts tab of the bench.
- Sample-size and ramp tests used throwaway scripts that import `eval/generate_data.py` and the `Engine` class in `eval/eval_temporal.py` (not committed).

## 13. Rain and events nearby, at 1.25x / 1.25x (per-ride-type data)

From `eval/pickup_sweep_v6.js` on the final defaults and the per-ride-type engine. Share of usual commute times that would get a ping:

| Window | Ride type | Dry | Rain | Event nearby | Rain + event |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| weekday morning (6:00-11:00) | Auto (three-wheeler) | 6.7% | 5.7% | 8.6% | 9.5% |
| weekday morning (6:00-11:00) | Cab (standard/sedan/six-seater) | 8.6% | 1.9% | 1.9% | 9.5% |
| weekday morning (6:00-11:00) | Two-wheeler | 0% | 10.5% | 1.9% | 12.4% |
| weekday evening (16:00-21:00) | Auto (three-wheeler) | 7.6% | 6.7% | 9.5% | 0% |
| weekday evening (16:00-21:00) | Cab (standard/sedan/six-seater) | 9.5% | 3.8% | 1.9% | 0% |
| weekday evening (16:00-21:00) | Two-wheeler | 2.9% | 13.3% | 7.6% | 10.5% |
| Saturday night (19:00-23:30) | Auto (three-wheeler) | 8.4% | 8.4% | 12.6% | 0% |
| Saturday night (19:00-23:30) | Cab (standard/sedan/six-seater) | 11.6% | 5.3% | 4.2% | 0% |
| Saturday night (19:00-23:30) | Two-wheeler | 1.1% | 12.6% | 2.1% | 12.6% |

Findings: cabs are pinged about 9-12% of dry commute times but only 2-5% with rain or an event and 0% in the evening with both, because surge is already above 1.25x 30 minutes before the usual time; autos hold at roughly 6-13% except 0% for evening and Saturday-night rain-plus-event; two-wheelers (now with their own data) are pinged about 0-3% dry and 10-13% in rain. The rule is a "surge is about to build" signal and goes silent when surge is already high. Full tables: `eval/pickup_sweep_v6_report.md`.

## 14. Re-run on the per-ride-type data: rule comparison and advice size

Weekday morning (6:00-11:00) and evening (16:00-21:00), 5 routes, every 15 minutes, each ride type on its own forecast. Share of usual commute times pinged:

| Ride type | Rule (trigger / ceiling) | Dry | Rain | Event | Rain + event |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cab (Standard) | 1.25 / 1.10 | 2.4% | 0% | 3.3% | 3.8% |
| Cab (Standard) | 1.25 / 1.20 | 7.1% | 1.4% | 4.3% | 4.8% |
| Cab (Standard) | **1.25 / 1.25** | **9.0%** | **4.3%** | **5.7%** | **4.8%** |
| Cab (Standard) | 1.40 / 1.25 | 1.9% | 1.0% | 2.4% | 4.8% |
| Cab (Standard) | 1.40 / 1.40 | 6.7% | 9.0% | 8.6% | 4.8% |
| Auto | 1.25 / 1.10 | 0% | 0.5% | 1.0% | 4.8% |
| Auto | 1.25 / 1.20 | 4.8% | 2.9% | 4.3% | 4.8% |
| Auto | **1.25 / 1.25** | **7.1%** | **7.1%** | **9.5%** | **4.8%** |
| Auto | 1.40 / 1.25 | 0% | 0% | 0% | 4.8% |
| Auto | 1.40 / 1.40 | 4.8% | 9.0% | 7.6% | 7.1% |
| Two-wheeler | 1.25 / 1.10 | 0% | 0% | 0% | 1.4% |
| Two-wheeler | 1.25 / 1.20 | 0.5% | 3.3% | 1.4% | 1.9% |
| Two-wheeler | **1.25 / 1.25** | **1.4%** | **11.9%** | **4.8%** | **11.4%** |
| Two-wheeler | 1.40 / 1.25 | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| Two-wheeler | 1.40 / 1.40 | 0% | 1.0% | 0% | 4.8% |

Findings: the same as before. The strict ceilings (1.1x, or a 1.4x trigger with a 1.25x ceiling) almost never fire; 1.25x / 1.25x pings the most while staying selective; 1.4x / 1.4x is comparable for cabs but nearly silent for dry-day autos and two-wheelers. Sedan behaves like the cab (1.25 / 1.25: 9.5% dry, 5.7% rain, 8.6% rain plus event).

**How much cheaper the earlier start is, when a ping fires at 1.25x / 1.25x** (all dry/rain/event cases, both peaks):

| Ride type | Pings | Smallest gap | Median gap | Largest gap | Under 0.05x | Under 0.10x |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cab | 50 | 0.02x | 0.22x | 0.83x | 2 | 5 |
| Auto | 60 | 0.02x | 0.11x | 0.54x | 5 | 25 |
| Two-wheeler | 62 | 0.00x | 0.05x | 0.25x | 22 | 57 |

So the advice is solid for cabs, borderline for autos (about 40% of pings have a gap under 0.10x) and weak for two-wheelers (most pings have a gap under 0.10x). The product owner chose not to add a minimum gap (the ping goes out at most once per direction per day); the wording "to avoid the surge" overstates the benefit for two-wheeler and some auto riders. This is the main known weakness of the chosen rule.

The sample-size test (5 seeds, up to 10x the rows) and the ramp-shape test (8 shapes) in Sections 8 and 9 were run on the earlier dataset; they showed the equal-threshold rule is robust, and Standard (cab) data is generated the same way now. They have not been repeated on the per-ride-type data.
